drills.los_text: explain the components of execution costs, including explicit and implicit costs

questions.stem: Explicit trading costs most likely include:

options.A: Market impact.
options.B: The bid-ask spread and delay costs.
options.C: Broker commissions, transaction taxes, stamp duties, and exchange fees.

rationales.A: Market impact is an implicit cost, not an explicit one. It is the effect of the trade on transaction prices, an indirect cost caused by the act of trading, and no one issues a bill for it. Explicit costs are the direct costs of trading, for which a trader could receive a receipt.
rationales.B: Both items are implicit costs. The bid-ask spread is the price concession an impatient trader makes to trade immediately, and delay costs arise from the inability to complete the desired trade immediately. Neither produces an invoice, so neither is explicit.
rationales.C: Explicit costs are the direct costs of trading, such as broker commission costs, transaction taxes, stamp duties, and fees paid to exchanges. They are costs for which a trader could receive a receipt, so they are visible and directly measurable from invoices. Implicit costs, by contrast, are the indirect costs caused by the market impact of trading and by the price concessions impatient traders make to complete trades.

questions.stem: Implicit trading costs most likely include:

options.A: The bid-ask spread, market impact, delay, and opportunity costs.
options.B: Transaction taxes.
options.C: Broker commissions.

rationales.A: Implicit costs are the indirect costs caused by the market impact of trading, and they have four components. The bid-ask spread is the price concession paid for immediacy. Market impact, or price impact, is the effect of the trade on transaction prices, as traders filling large orders must move prices to encourage others to trade with them. Delay costs, also called slippage, arise from the inability to complete the desired trade immediately. Opportunity costs, or unrealized profit and loss, arise from the failure to execute a trade promptly. So the set is spread, market impact, delay, and opportunity cost.
rationales.B: Transaction taxes are explicit costs. They are direct costs of trading for which a trader could receive a receipt, not indirect costs caused by the market impact of trading.
rationales.C: Broker commissions are explicit costs. They are billed and invoiced, which is exactly what separates explicit costs from implicit ones.

questions.stem: The bid-ask spread is most likely:

options.A: The ask price minus the bid price.
options.B: The midpoint between the standing bid and ask.
options.C: The discount rate dealers apply when financing inventory.

rationales.A: The bid-ask spread is the ask price, the price at which a trader will sell a specified quantity of a security, minus the bid price, the price at which a trader will buy a specified quantity of a security. Traders who want to trade quickly buy at higher prices and sell at lower prices than those willing to wait for others to trade with them, so the spread measures the size of that concession.
rationales.B: The midpoint of the standing bid and ask is a reference price, the midquote, which serves as the benchmark in transaction cost estimates such as the effective spread. The spread itself is the difference between the two quotes, ask minus bid, not their average.
rationales.C: Dealer financing rates are a separate element of dealer economics. The spread is the gap between the price at which a trader will sell a specified quantity and the price at which a trader will buy it.

questions.stem: Market impact (price impact) is most likely:

options.A: A cost incurred only on small trades.
options.B: The effect of a trade on transaction prices.
options.C: A cost of zero in continuously quoted liquid markets.

rationales.A: Impact grows with order size rather than shrinking with it. Small market orders generally have small market impact because they are often filled immediately by traders willing to trade at the quoted bid and offer prices, or even at better prices. Larger orders have greater market impact because the trader must move the market to fill them.
rationales.B: Market impact, or price impact, is the effect of the trade on transaction prices. Traders who want to fill large orders often must move prices to encourage others to trade with them. For small orders, market impact is often limited to buying at ask prices and selling at bid prices, and small market orders generally have small impact because they are filled immediately by traders willing to trade at the quoted prices. Larger orders require larger price concessions, so impact rises with order size relative to available liquidity.
rationales.C: Impact is a real and measurable cost even in the most liquid, continuously quoted markets. Liquidity reduces the price concession required to fill an order; it does not eliminate it, and an order large relative to available liquidity still moves prices.

questions.stem: Delay costs (slippage) most likely arise from:

options.A: The commissions brokers charge for handling orders.
options.B: The inability to complete the desired trade immediately.
options.C: The instant of order submission.

rationales.A: Commissions are explicit costs, billed by the broker for handling the order. Delay costs are implicit and arise from the inability to trade immediately, so they are incurred whether or not any commission is paid.
rationales.B: Delay costs, also called slippage, arise from the inability to complete the desired trade immediately because of the order's size in relation to available market liquidity. Traders fail to profit when they fill their orders after prices have already moved as they expected. Delay costs also arise when portfolio managers or their traders fail to create and route orders quickly to the markets where they will fill most quickly. Analysts often measure delay costs on the portion of the order carried over from one day to the next. Delay is costly when the price moves away from an order, up for a buy order and down for a sell order, often because information leaks into the market.
rationales.C: No cost is locked in at submission. The cost accrues as prices move away from the order during the delay, and it is realized when the order fills after prices have already run. An order filled immediately at submission incurs no delay cost at all.

questions.stem: Opportunity costs most likely arise from:

options.A: The failure to execute a trade promptly.
options.B: The broker commissions paid on completed trades.
options.C: The trades that execute successfully at favorable prices.

rationales.A: Opportunity costs, or unrealized profit and loss, arise from the failure to execute a trade promptly. Traders fail to profit when their orders fail to trade and prices move as they expect. These costs are often significant for large orders, and when delays in execution cause a portion of the order to go unfilled, the associated cost is called opportunity cost. They are difficult to measure, being sensitive to the time frame chosen and to assumptions about the prices at which the orders could have traded.
rationales.B: Commissions are explicit costs paid on trades that were actually done. Opportunity cost is the profit missed on orders that were never filled and would have paid off, so it is incurred precisely where no commission is charged.
rationales.C: A trade that completes at a favorable price incurs no opportunity cost. The cost belongs to the portion of the order that fails to trade while prices move as the trader expected.

questions.stem: For buy-side institutions, fixed trading costs most likely include:

options.A: Trader salaries, trading systems and data, and office space.
options.B: No fixed costs of any kind.
options.C: Commissions only.

rationales.A: The costs of trading include fixed costs and variable costs. For buy-side institutions, fixed trading costs include the costs of employing buy-side traders, the costs of equipping them with proper trading tools such as electronic systems and data, and the costs of office space, whether full trading rooms or trading corners. Small buy-side institutions often avoid these costs by not employing buy-side traders at all, with their portfolio managers submitting orders directly to their brokers.
rationales.B: Employing buy-side traders, equipping them with electronic systems and data, and housing them in trading rooms are all real fixed costs, incurred whether or not any order is sent that day. Only the smallest institutions avoid them, by having portfolio managers route orders directly to brokers.
rationales.C: Commissions are variable transaction costs: they arise from trading activity and scale with it. The fixed base consists of people, systems, data, and space.

questions.stem: Dealer A quotes a bid of 98.85 and an ask of 100.51, Dealer B a bid of 98.84 and an ask of 100.55, and Dealer C a bid of 98.82 and an ask of 100.49. The market spread is closest to:

rationales.A: 1.66 is Dealer A's own spread, 100.51 - 98.85. The market spread is not any individual dealer's spread; it is built from the best bid across all dealers and the best ask across all dealers, which here come from two different dealers.
rationales.B: 1.71 is Dealer B's individual spread, 100.55 - 98.84. The market spread uses the best bid, 98.85 from Dealer A, and the best ask, 100.49 from Dealer C: 100.49 - 98.85 = 1.64.
rationales.C: The best bid price, 98.85 by Dealer A, is lower than the best ask price, 100.49 by Dealer C, so the market spread is 100.49 - 98.85 = 1.64. That is lower than any of the individual dealers' spreads, which are 1.66 for A, 1.71 for B, and 1.67 for C, because the dealer posting the highest bid is not the dealer posting the lowest ask. The corresponding midquote is (100.49 + 98.85)/2 = 99.67.

drills.los_text: calculate and interpret effective spreads and VWAP transaction cost estimates

questions.stem: For a buy order, the effective spread is most likely:

options.A: The gap between the trade price and the midquote at order entry.
options.B: Twice the gap between the trade price and the VWAP benchmark.
options.C: Twice the gap between the trade price and the midquote at order entry.

rationales.A: Trade price minus midquote at order entry is the midquote price benchmark estimate of transaction cost for a buy, but it is not the effective spread. The effective spread doubles that quantity: 2 x (trade price - midquote at order entry).
rationales.B: The effective spread is measured from the midquote at the time of order entry, not from a VWAP benchmark. VWAP is a separate benchmark-price method of estimating transaction costs, computed against the volume-weighted average price over an interval rather than against the quote standing when the order was entered.
rationales.C: Multiplying the midquote price benchmark transaction cost estimate by 2 produces the effective spread: for a purchase, 2 x (trade price - midquote at order entry), and for a sale, 2 x (midquote at order entry - trade price). It is the spread that traders would have observed if the quoted ask, for a purchase, or the quoted bid, for a sale, had been equal to the trade price. The effective spread is a sensible estimate of transaction costs when orders are filled in single trades. Equivalently, effective spread = 2 x the absolute value of (trade price - midquote at order entry).

questions.stem: Price improvement most likely occurs when:

options.A: An order fills at a price outside the quoted spread.
options.B: Execution prices are always worse than the quoted prices.
options.C: Execution prices are better than the quoted prices.

rationales.A: An order that fills at a price outside the quoted spread has an effective spread that is larger than the quoted spread. That is the opposite result, and it occurs when trade execution prices are worse than quoted prices. Price improvement is a fill better than the quote: a buy below the ask or a sell above the bid.
rationales.B: This states the opposite of price improvement. When execution prices are worse than the quoted prices, the order fills outside the quoted spread and the effective spread is larger than the quoted spread. Improvement means the fill beats the standing quote, and it is not inevitable in either direction.
rationales.C: Price improvement occurs when trade execution prices are better than quoted prices. If an order fills at a price better than the quoted price, for example a buy order filling below the ask price or a sell order filling above the bid price, the order is said to receive price improvement and the spread is effectively lower, so the effective spread is less than the quoted spread.

questions.stem: The effective spread is most likely a poor estimate of transaction costs when orders are:

options.A: split into many parts filled over time.
options.B: nonexistent in the market.
options.C: always filled immediately in single executions.

rationales.A: Traders split large orders into many parts to fill over time, and such orders often move the market, causing bid and ask prices to rise or fall. The impact of the order on market prices, called market impact, makes trading expensive — especially for the last parts to fill — but the effective spread will not fully identify this cost if it is computed separately for each trade. Each fill is measured against a midquote that the earlier parts of the same order have already pushed away, so the cumulative cost of working the order is spread across trades and never aggregated.
rationales.B: A market with no orders produces no trades and no quotes, so there is no effective spread to compute and nothing to estimate badly. The failure case is real and common rather than hypothetical: large orders split into parts and filled over time move the quotes, and an effective spread computed trade by trade misses that cumulative market impact.
rationales.C: Immediate single fills are where the effective spread works best. The trade price can be compared directly with the midquote prevailing at order entry, no earlier part of the order has moved that midquote, and twice the distance between them is a clean measure of the round-trip cost. The measure breaks down in the opposite case, when a large order is worked in pieces over an extended period.

questions.curriculum_ref: Effective Spread — poor for split orders

questions.stem: A market sell order for 2,000 shares is filled at C$10.15 when the market is C$10.12 bid and C$10.24 ask. The effective spread on the trade is closest to:

rationales.A: C$0.24 is twice the quoted spread of C$0.12, and it is also the ask price. The doubling in the effective spread formula applies to the distance between the midquote and the trade price, not to the quoted spread itself, so the quoted spread is never doubled to produce an effective spread.
rationales.B: The effective spread for a sell order is 2 × (Midpoint of the market at the time of order entry − Trade price). The midpoint of the market at order entry is (C$10.12 + C$10.24)/2 = C$10.18, so the effective spread is 2 × (C$10.18 − C$10.15) = C$0.06. Because the effective spread of C$0.06 is less than the quoted spread of C$0.12, the order received price improvement: it sold at C$10.15, above the C$10.12 bid it could have hit.
rationales.C: C$0.12 is the quoted spread, C$10.24 − C$10.12. The effective spread measures what this particular trade actually gave up relative to the midquote at order entry, and here it came in at half the quoted spread because the sale executed above the bid rather than at it.

questions.stem: For a buy order, the VWAP transaction cost estimate is most likely:

options.A: the trade size times the excess of the benchmark VWAP over the trade VWAP.
options.B: the trade size times the excess of the trade VWAP over the benchmark VWAP.
options.C: twice the excess of the trade VWAP over the midquote at order entry.

rationales.A: The sign is reversed. For a buy, the cost is Trade size × (Trade VWAP − VWAP benchmark), which is positive when the fills average above the benchmark, because paying more than the market's average price is the cost. Trade size × (VWAP benchmark − Trade VWAP) is the formula for a sell, where selling below the benchmark is what hurts.
rationales.B: For a buy: Trade size × (Trade VWAP − VWAP benchmark). For a sell: Trade size × (VWAP benchmark − Trade VWAP). Volume-weighted average price is one of the most widely used benchmark prices that analysts use to estimate transaction costs. Analysts typically compute the VWAP using all trades that occurred from the start of the order until the order was completed, a measure often referred to as interval VWAP. The VWAP is the sum of the total dollar value of the benchmark trades divided by the total quantity of those trades.
rationales.C: Doubling the difference between the trade price and the midquote at order entry is the effective spread calculation, not the VWAP transaction cost estimate. The VWAP estimate compares the trade VWAP with the interval VWAP benchmark and scales that per-share difference by the number of shares traded; there is no doubling and no reference to the entry midquote.

questions.stem: A mutual fund sells 10,000 shares at an average price of C$10.0680. Total volume that day is 13,000 shares: 2,000 at C$10.15, 3,000 at C$10.11, 5,000 at C$10.01, 2,000 at C$10.20, and 1,000 at C$10.15. The VWAP transaction cost estimate for the sale is closest to:

rationales.A: C$10,000 is the wrong order of magnitude. The estimate is the per-share gap between the two VWAPs multiplied by the 10,000 shares sold, and that gap is under three cents, so the answer lands in the hundreds of dollars. A cost near C$10,000 on proceeds of about C$100,700 would imply a price concession of roughly C$1 per share.
rationales.B: A zero estimate would require the trade VWAP to equal the VWAP benchmark. Here the fund sold at an average of C$10.0680 against a full-day VWAP of C$10.0946, so its fills averaged below the market's own average price for the interval and the measured cost is real and positive.
rationales.C: The VWAP for the day is the total dollar volume divided by the total number of shares traded. Dollar volume is 2,000 × C$10.15 + 3,000 × C$10.11 + 5,000 × C$10.01 + 2,000 × C$10.20 + 1,000 × C$10.15 = C$131,230. Dividing by the 13,000-share total volume gives a VWAP benchmark of C$10.0946. A similar calculation using only the sales made by the mutual fund gives a trade VWAP of C$10.0680. The VWAP transaction cost estimate for the sale is the difference multiplied by the 10,000 shares sold: 10,000 × (C$10.0946 − C$10.0680) = C$266.15.

questions.stem: Interpreting a VWAP transaction cost estimate is most likely problematic because the estimate is:

options.A: always exactly zero by construction.
options.B: biased toward zero when the evaluated trades dominate the benchmark.
options.C: impossible to interpret under any conditions.

rationales.A: The bias is toward zero, not an identity. Only in the limiting case — a large trader who is the only buyer for a given interval — does the estimate collapse to zero regardless of market impact. A trade that is small relative to the interval's volume and poorly timed against it will still show a positive measured cost.
rationales.B: Interpreting VWAP transaction cost estimates is problematic when the trades being evaluated are a substantial fraction of all trades in the VWAP benchmark, or, more generally, when the trades took place at the same rate as other trades in the market. In both cases the trade VWAP and the VWAP benchmark will be nearly equal, which suggests that the evaluated trades were not costly. That conclusion is misleading if the trade had substantial price impact: if a large trader were the only buyer for a given trading period, the estimate would be zero regardless of the impact. This bias toward zero helps explain why the measure is so popular, since investment managers like to show sponsors cost estimates suggesting that trading is not expensive.
rationales.C: The estimates are interpretable; they are simply biased in identifiable situations. Knowing that the bias runs toward zero when the evaluated trades make up much of the benchmark volume, or trade at the same rate as the rest of the market, tells an analyst exactly when to discount a flattering VWAP number and when to trust it.

questions.stem: A large sell order exceeds the size available at the bid and walks down the limit order book. Measured against the quoted spread, the effective spread on that order is most likely:

options.A: less than the quoted spread.
options.B: greater than the quoted spread.
options.C: equal to the quoted spread.

rationales.A: The direction is the reverse. An effective spread below the quoted spread signals price improvement, which happens when an order fills inside the quote. Walking down the book is the opposite: successive shares fill at successively worse prices, which widens the effective spread beyond the quote.
rationales.B: The effective spread for the order is greater than the quoted spread because the large order size, which was greater than the bid size, caused the order to walk down the limit order book. The average sale price was less than the bid, so the effective spread — twice the distance from the midquote at order entry to the average trade price — was higher than the quoted spread. Walking the book adds market impact on top of the quoted spread.
rationales.C: Equality holds only when the fill completes at the quote, as for a small market order executed exactly at the prevailing bid or ask. Once the order size exceeds the displayed bid size, the remaining shares must take liquidity at lower limit prices, and the average sale price falls below the bid.

drills.los_text: describe the implementation shortfall approach to transaction cost measurement

questions.stem: Implementation shortfall most likely measures:

options.A: the total cost of implementing an investment decision, explicit and implicit.
options.B: only the market impact component of trading cost.
options.C: only the commissions paid on executed trades.

rationales.A: The implementation shortfall method of measuring trading costs addresses the problems associated with the effective spread method. It is attractive because it views trading from an investment management perspective and measures the total cost of implementing an investment decision by capturing all explicit and implicit costs. The method includes market impact costs and delay costs as well as opportunity costs, which are often significant for large orders.
rationales.B: Market impact is only one of the components captured. Implementation shortfall measures impact alongside delay costs and the opportunity cost of shares never filled, which is what makes it the total cost of implementing the decision rather than one piece of it.
rationales.C: Commissions are a single explicit slice. Implementation shortfall is comprehensive: explicit costs such as commissions together with implicit costs — market impact, delay, and opportunity cost — all measured against the value of a paper portfolio transacted at the decision price.

questions.stem: Implementation shortfall most likely compares:

options.A: the target portfolio with the planning document.
options.B: the actual portfolio with its benchmark index.
options.C: the actual portfolio with a paper portfolio transacted at decision prices.

rationales.A: The comparison is between the actual portfolio and a paper portfolio transacted at the decision prices, not between a target holding and a planning document. Nothing in the measure references the policy statement; its inputs are the decision-time midquote, the actual fill prices, and the shares actually filled.
rationales.B: Comparing a portfolio with its benchmark index measures relative performance, not trading cost. Implementation shortfall holds the investment decision fixed and asks what executing it cost, by comparing the actual portfolio with the paper portfolio built at decision prices.
rationales.C: Implementation shortfall compares the values of the actual portfolio with that of a paper portfolio constructed on the assumption that trades could be arranged at the prices that prevailed when the decision to trade is made. The prevailing price — also called the decision price, the arrival price, or the strike price — is generally taken to be the midquote price at the time of the trade decision. The excess of the paper value over the actual value is the implementation shortfall.

questions.stem: The decision price, also called the arrival price or the strike price, is most likely:

options.A: the midquote at the time of the trade decision.
options.B: the closing price.
options.C: the ask price.

rationales.A: The prevailing price — also called the decision price, the arrival price, or the strike price — is generally taken to be the midquote price at the time of the trade decision. Fixing that reference point is what allows the paper portfolio, which assumes every share transacts at the decision price, to be compared fairly with the actual portfolio; the excess of the paper value over the actual value is the implementation shortfall.
rationales.B: The closing price is not the reference. The decision price is struck at the moment the decision to trade is made, so that everything after it is attributable to implementation. A closing price would fold in a full session of market movement that has nothing to do with how the order was worked.
rationales.C: The midquote, not the ask, is the convention. Measuring from the ask would build half the quoted spread into the reference price itself, so the spread cost of a buy would disappear from the measured shortfall; the midquote is also neutral between buys and sells.

questions.stem: Implementation shortfall is most likely preferred over effective spread when:

options.A: orders always fill in single executions.
options.B: orders are large and split over time.
options.C: no orders exist in the market.

rationales.A: Single immediate fills are the effective spread's home turf. The trade price can be compared directly with the midquote at order entry, there is no earlier fill that has moved the quote, and no delay or opportunity cost arises, so the simpler measure captures essentially the whole cost.
rationales.B: The implementation shortfall method addresses the problems associated with the effective spread method. It includes market impact costs and delay costs as well as opportunity costs, which are often significant for large orders. When an order is large and worked in pieces over an extended period, prices move away during execution; an effective spread computed separately for each trade measures each fill against an already-moved midquote and so understates the cumulative market impact, and it ignores altogether the shares that were never filled.
rationales.C: A market with no orders produces no trades and no cost to measure, so it cannot be the case where one measure is preferred to another. The genuine preference case is large orders split over time, where implementation shortfall captures the impact, delay, and opportunity costs that a per-trade effective spread misses.

questions.stem: The paper portfolio used to measure implementation shortfall most likely assumes:

options.A: Worst-case prices.
options.B: Decision-time prices.
options.C: Actual execution prices.

rationales.A: Worst-case prices are not the paper portfolio's benchmark. The paper portfolio is a frictionless counterfactual, not a conservative or adverse-case construction: it holds prices fixed at the decision point rather than assuming the least favorable prices observed while the order was being worked.
rationales.B: Implementation shortfall compares the value of the actual portfolio with that of a paper portfolio constructed on the assumption that trades could be arranged at the prices that prevailed when the decision to trade was made. That hypothetical benchmark measures what would have been achieved with instant, frictionless execution: no market impact, no delay, and no opportunity cost on unfilled orders. The gap between the paper portfolio and the actual portfolio therefore isolates the cost of implementation.
rationales.C: Actual execution prices describe the real portfolio, not the paper one. The paper portfolio is built on hypothetical prices, the decision-time prices, and if it used the actual fills instead there would be no difference left to measure as a shortfall.

questions.stem: The excess of a paper portfolio's value over the actual portfolio's value is most likely:

options.A: A negative amount in every case.
options.B: The portfolio's realized return.
options.C: The implementation shortfall.

rationales.A: The difference is typically positive, because implementation normally costs something: commissions and taxes, spread and market impact, delay, and opportunity cost on unfilled orders all push the actual portfolio's value below the paper portfolio's. A negative figure is possible when prices happen to move favorably after the decision, but it is not the usual sign and certainly not an invariable one.
rationales.B: The difference is a cost measure, not a return. Return is computed from the actual portfolio's own beginning and ending values; the paper-versus-actual gap compares two portfolios over the same interval and isolates what execution cost. It is a drag on the realized return rather than the return itself.
rationales.C: The excess of the paper value over the actual value is the implementation shortfall. A positive number represents the total costs of implementation, and a larger difference means more implementation cost. The measure can be decomposed into explicit costs such as commissions and taxes, market impact and spread costs, delay costs, and opportunity costs on the portion of the order that went unfilled, which lets a trader identify which parts of the process are the most costly.

questions.stem: Relative to the effective spread, implementation shortfall is most likely:

options.A: Broader in cost coverage.
options.B: Simpler to compute.
options.C: Equivalent, as the effective spread omits nothing.

rationales.A: The effective spread is computed trade by trade, so it misses the market impact that accumulates when a large order is split across many trades, the delay cost between the decision and the first fill, and the opportunity cost of the portion never filled, all of which are often significant for large orders. The implementation shortfall method addresses exactly these problems: it includes market impact costs and delay costs as well as opportunity costs, measuring the total decision-to-execution drag on portfolio performance rather than slippage on an individual trade.
rationales.B: Implementation shortfall is more complex to compute, not simpler: it requires a decision price, the full record of fills and their timing, and a valuation of the unfilled remainder, whereas the effective spread needs only a trade price and a reference midquote. Its advantage is comprehensiveness across impact, delay, and unfilled-order costs, not computational ease.
rationales.C: The effective spread does have limitations, demonstrably so on split orders, where its per-trade calculation cannot aggregate cross-trade market impact and where delay and opportunity costs are ignored entirely. There is a real gap for implementation shortfall to address.

drills.los_text: describe factors driving the development of electronic trading systems

questions.stem: The widespread use of electronic trading systems most likely has:

options.A: Raised buy-side trading costs materially.
options.B: Left buy-side trading costs unchanged.
options.C: Lowered buy-side trading costs.

rationales.A: This reverses the observed direction. Electronic systems lowered the cost of matching trades rather than raising it, and competition among liquidity providers passed those savings on to buy-side traders.
rationales.B: The impact was substantial, not neutral. Exchanges obtained materially greater cost efficiencies from electronic matching, and those efficiencies showed up in the spreads buy-side traders paid.
rationales.C: The widespread use of electronic trading systems significantly decreased trading costs for buy-side traders. Costs fell as exchanges obtained greater cost efficiencies from using electronic matching systems instead of floor-based, manual trading systems. The same technologies decreased costs and increased efficiencies for the dealers and arbitrageurs who provide much of the liquidity offered at exchanges, and competition forced them to pass along many of the benefits of their new technologies to buy-side traders in the form of narrower spreads quoted for larger sizes.

questions.stem: Compared with floor-based trading systems, electronic order-matching systems most likely offer:

options.A: No advantages.
options.B: One advantage, longer trading hours.
options.C: Many advantages.

rationales.A: The advantages are numerous and decisive across cost, precision, record keeping, speed, and scale. Human floor brokers can negotiate nuances, but that does not leave electronic systems with no advantage; it is one narrow offset against a long list.
rationales.B: Longer hours are only one item on that list. Electronic systems are also cheap to operate, enforce precedence and pricing rules without error, keep perfect audit trails, and keep hidden orders genuinely hidden, so they do not merely match floors on cost, accuracy, and record keeping.
rationales.C: Compared with floor-based trading systems, electronic order-matching systems enjoy many advantages. Most obviously, they are cheap to operate once built: operating in server rooms, they require less physical space than trading floors. They do exactly what they are programmed to do, so when properly programmed they precisely enforce the exchange's trading order precedence and pricing rules without error or exception, and they can keep perfect audit trails. Electronic systems that support hidden orders keep those orders perfectly hidden; unlike floor brokers, they never inadvertently or fraudulently reveal a client's hidden orders to others. They can operate, for the most part, on a continuous, around-the-clock basis, and they can keep operating when bad weather or other events would prevent workers from convening on a floor.

questions.stem: Computers dominate the implementation of many trading strategies most likely because they possess:

options.A: Attention, speed, discipline, and memory.
options.B: No capability relevant to strategy implementation.
options.C: Human intuition.

rationales.A: Computers have come to dominate the implementation of many trading strategies because they are so efficient and so unlike human traders. They have infinite attention spans and a very wide attention scope, continuously watching and responding to information from many instruments and many markets simultaneously and essentially forever. Their responses are extraordinarily fast. They are perfectly disciplined and do only what they are instructed, that is programmed, to do. And they do not forget any information that their programmers want to save.
rationales.B: The relevant capabilities are substantial: infinite attention spans, simultaneous monitoring of many instruments and markets, and instant, flawless execution of the instructions they are given.
rationales.C: Intuition is precisely what computers lack. Their edge over human traders lies in attention span and scope, speed of response, programmed discipline, and perfect retention, not in judgment or insight.

questions.stem: Order-driven markets are best described as:

options.A: Paper-based markets that predate electronic trading.
options.B: Dealer-only markets in which customers cannot post orders.
options.C: Markets that match submitted orders by rule.

rationales.A: Modern order-driven markets are overwhelmingly electronic. What defines them is the rules-based matching system, not the medium: electronic trading systems have largely displaced floor-based systems in all instruments for which order-driven markets are viable.
rationales.B: Dealer-centric quoting describes the quote-driven model, in which customers trade against dealer quotes. Order-driven markets match orders submitted by traders, including customers, under the venue's precedence and pricing rules.
rationales.C: Order-driven markets are markets in which orders submitted by traders are arranged based on a rules-based, order-matching system run by an exchange, a broker, or an alternative trading system (ATS). They are now organized by most exchanges and by electronic communication networks (ECNs), having largely displaced floor-based trading in every instrument for which the order-driven structure is viable.

questions.stem: Relative to equities, futures, and options markets, electronic trading in corporate and municipal bond markets is most likely:

options.A: Equally advanced.
options.B: Unviable, given bond market structure.
options.C: Less advanced.

rationales.A: Bond electronification lags rather than matches. Much less attention has been given to the market structures of corporate and municipal bond markets, most of which, from the customer's point of view, have changed little since the late 19th century.
rationales.B: The potential is substantial, not absent. The lag reflects instrument heterogeneity, above all the fact that bond issues, especially municipal bonds, vastly outnumber stock issues, rather than any structural impossibility.
rationales.C: The electronification of bond markets has lagged that of the equities, futures, and options markets. Despite the efforts of many creative developers of electronic bond trading systems, most public investors in these markets still trade largely over the counter with dealers. The potential for electronic trading systems here, and the attendant growth in electronic trading strategies, is quite large, and such systems will undoubtedly have to reflect the fact that bond issues, especially municipal bonds, vastly outnumber stock issues.

questions.stem: The two co-dependent systems essential to electronic trading are most likely:

options.A: Regulatory surveillance systems and consolidated tape feeds.
options.B: Traders' order systems and exchanges' matching systems.
options.C: Clearinghouse settlement systems and floor-broker networks.

rationales.A: Surveillance systems and consolidated data feeds support oversight and reporting rather than the trading process itself. The co-dependent pair is traders' high-speed order processing and communication systems together with the exchanges' electronic exchange systems.
rationales.B: The two types of systems are co-dependent: traders need high-speed order processing and communication systems to implement their electronic trading strategies, and the exchanges need electronic exchange systems to process the vast numbers of orders that these electronic traders produce. The adoption of electronic exchange systems is what led to the huge growth in automated order creation and submission systems on the trader side.
rationales.C: Clearing and settlement follow trading rather than enabling it, and floor-broker communication networks belong to manual markets. The co-dependent pair is traders' high-speed order processing and communication systems and the exchanges' electronic exchange systems.

questions.stem: As electronic trading has grown, studies of transaction costs most likely show:

options.A: No change in transaction costs.
options.B: Declining transaction costs.
options.C: Rising transaction costs.

rationales.A: Costs did not hold steady; they declined significantly, both over time and across venues, as electronic trading spread.
rationales.B: Numerous studies show that transaction costs declined with the growth of electronic trading over time. Some studies also show that at a given point in time, lower transaction costs are found in those markets with the greatest intensity of electronic trading. These time-series and cross-sectional results are not surprising: they follow from the greater cost efficiencies associated with electronic trading. With that growth, bid-ask spreads decreased substantially, which lowered transaction costs for retail traders and for institutions trading small orders.
rationales.C: Costs declined rather than rose. Bid-ask spreads narrowed substantially as electronic trading grew, and the markets with the most intense electronic trading are the ones with the lowest measured costs.

questions.stem: Market fragmentation most likely means:

options.A: Concentration of all trading in a single exchange.
options.B: An absence of trading venues for the instrument.
options.C: Trading of the same instrument in multiple venues.

rationales.A: Concentration of order flow in one venue is the opposite of fragmentation. Fragmentation is the condition in which venues trading the same instruments have proliferated, so that trading in any given instrument now occurs across many venues rather than in one place.
rationales.B: Fragmentation implies a proliferation of venues, not their absence. Markets for many asset classes have become increasingly fragmented throughout the world precisely because the number of venues trading the same instruments has grown; an instrument with no venue at all would not trade.
rationales.C: Market fragmentation is trading the same instrument in multiple venues. Markets for many asset classes have become increasingly fragmented throughout the world because venues trading the same instruments have proliferated and trading in any given instrument now occurs in multiple venues. Available liquidity for an instrument on any one exchange now often represents just a small fraction of the aggregate liquidity for that instrument. Fragmentation increases the potential for price and liquidity disparities across venues, because buyers and sellers often are not in the same venue at the same time, which is what creates the need for liquidity aggregation and smart order routing.

questions.stem: In the US, exchange-listed equities order flow is most likely:

options.A: Concentrated on 3 primary exchanges and a few regional exchanges.
options.B: Divided among 11 exchanges and numerous dealers, with no alternative trading systems.
options.C: Divided among 11 exchanges, 40 alternative trading systems, and numerous dealers.

rationales.A: That describes the late 20th century, when trading mainly occurred on three primary exchanges, a few minor regional exchanges, and in the offices of some large institutional broker/dealers. US order flow in exchange-listed equities is now far more fragmented than that.
rationales.B: Alternative trading systems do trade exchange-listed equities, and about 40 of them now take a share of US order flow. Also known as electronic communication networks (ECNs) or multilateral trading facilities (MTFs), they are increasingly important trading venues: they function like exchanges but do not exercise regulatory authority over their subscribers except concerning the conduct of trading in their own systems. Excluding them understates the degree of fragmentation.
rationales.C: In the United States, order flow in exchange-listed equities is now divided among 11 exchanges, 40 alternative trading systems, and numerous dealers. In the late 20th century, by contrast, trading mainly occurred on three primary exchanges, a few minor regional exchanges, and in the offices of some large institutional broker/dealers. The alternative trading systems, also known as electronic communication networks (ECNs) or multilateral trading facilities (MTFs), function like exchanges but do not exercise regulatory authority over their subscribers except concerning the conduct of their trading in their trading systems.

questions.stem: Alternative trading systems (ATSs) are most likely also known as:

options.A: Traditional exchanges.
options.B: Electronic communication networks or multilateral trading facilities.
options.C: Brokerages.

rationales.A: An ATS is not a traditional exchange. It functions like an exchange in matching its subscribers' orders, but it does not exercise regulatory authority over those subscribers except concerning the conduct of their trading within its own trading system, which is exactly what distinguishes it from a registered exchange.
rationales.B: Alternative trading systems (ATSs) are also known as electronic communication networks (ECNs) or multilateral trading facilities (MTFs). They are increasingly important trading venues: in US exchange-listed equities, about 40 of them share order flow with 11 exchanges and numerous dealers. They function like exchanges but do not exercise regulatory authority over their subscribers except concerning the conduct of their trading in their trading systems.
rationales.C: An ATS is a trading venue, not a brokerage. A broker acts as an agent, taking a client's order and routing it to venues for execution; an ATS is one of the venues where such an order can be filled, matching its subscribers' orders in the manner of an exchange.

questions.stem: Liquidity aggregators most likely:

options.A: Route each order to the venue displaying the greatest volume.
options.B: Create "super books" presenting liquidity across markets.
options.C: Merge all resting orders into one exchange's limit order book.

rationales.A: Routing orders among venues describes smart order routing, not liquidity aggregation. Smart order-routing algorithms send orders to the markets that display the best-quoted prices and sizes; liquidity aggregators do not route orders at all, they assemble a consolidated view of the liquidity available across all venues.
rationales.B: Liquidity aggregators create "super books" that present liquidity across markets for a given instrument. These tools offer global views of market depth, that is, of available liquidity, for each instrument regardless of which trading venue offers that liquidity. Together with smart order routing, they are the electronic algorithmic techniques that help traders manage the challenges and opportunities presented by fragmentation.
rationales.C: Aggregators do not physically merge orders into a single book. The orders remain at their original trading venues under those venues' rules and queues; what the aggregator supplies is a global view of market depth across venues, assembled for the trader's screen.

questions.stem: Smart order-routing algorithms most likely:

options.A: Send orders to the markets displaying the best-quoted prices and sizes.
options.B: Send all orders to the security's primary listing exchange.
options.C: Send orders to the venue charging the lowest access fees.

rationales.A: Smart order-routing algorithms send orders to the markets that display the best-quoted prices and sizes, which is how they help traders obtain best execution in a fragmented market. For example, the best bid for a Eurodollar future may be at CME while the second-best sits at ELX Markets, a fully electronic futures exchange; the router directs the order to the best-priced venue.
rationales.B: Routing everything to the listing exchange ignores fragmentation. The best bid or offer may be displayed on another exchange or on an alternative trading system, and the liquidity available on any one exchange is often just a small fraction of the aggregate. A smart router therefore directs orders to whichever market displays the best-quoted prices and sizes.
rationales.C: Smart order routers select venues by the best displayed prices and sizes, not by access fees. A low-fee venue showing an inferior quote would not receive the order, because the price concession would typically swamp the fee saving.

questions.stem: Traders filling large orders in fragmented markets most likely:

options.A: Concentrate all activity in a single venue.
options.B: Execute the entire order at once in one block.
options.C: Search for liquidity across multiple venues and over time.

rationales.A: Concentrating in one venue ignores the liquidity scattered across the others. Available liquidity for an instrument on any one exchange now often represents just a small fraction of the aggregate liquidity for that instrument, so a large order worked in a single venue would exhaust the depth there and move the price against the trader.
rationales.B: Executing all at once maximizes market impact rather than controlling it. The adaptation to fragmentation is to search across venues and across time: algorithms break the order into pieces and submit them to different markets over an interval, so that no single venue or moment absorbs the whole size.
rationales.C: With increasing market fragmentation, traders filling large orders now adapt their trading strategies to search for liquidity across multiple venues and across time, in order to control the market impacts of their trades. Algorithms break the order into pieces and submit them across markets over time. Electronic algorithmic trading techniques such as liquidity aggregation, which creates "super books" presenting liquidity across markets, and smart order routing, which sends orders to the markets displaying the best-quoted prices and sizes, help traders manage the challenges and opportunities presented by fragmentation.

questions.stem: Available liquidity for an instrument on any single exchange most likely:

options.A: Represents a small fraction of the instrument's aggregate liquidity.
options.B: Represents all of the instrument's aggregate liquidity.
options.C: Reveals nothing about the instrument's tradability.

rationales.A: Available liquidity for an instrument on any one exchange now often represents just a small fraction of the aggregate liquidity for that instrument, because venues trading the same instruments have proliferated and trading in any given instrument occurs in multiple venues. That is the challenge motivating the development of liquidity aggregation, which builds a global view of market depth across venues, and smart order routing, which sends orders to the best-quoted markets.
rationales.B: Fragmentation means each venue holds only a slice of the total, and often a small one. Were a single exchange's book the whole of the instrument's liquidity, there would be no price or liquidity disparities across venues and no need for aggregation tools or smart routers.
rationales.C: A single venue's displayed depth is real but partial information: it is a fraction of the cross-venue aggregate, not a null signal. Read alongside the other venues' books, through an aggregated "super book," it contributes to the global view of market depth for the instrument.

drills.los_text: identify and contrast the types of electronic traders

questions.stem: High-frequency traders (HFTs) most likely:

options.A: Hold positions for months.
options.B: Complete round trips within a minute, often within milliseconds.
options.C: Trade only once a year, at index reconstitution.

rationales.A: Holding for months is conventional investing, not high-frequency trading. An HFT round trip completes within a minute and often within a few milliseconds; even low-latency traders, who are slower than HFTs, hold positions for at most a day and sometimes a little longer.
rationales.B: High-frequency traders generally complete round trips composed of a purchase followed by a sale, or a sale followed by a purchase, within a minute and often as quickly as a few milliseconds. During a day they may trade in and out of an actively traded security or contract more than a thousand times, but usually only in small sizes.
rationales.C: HFT activity is continuous and extremely short-horizon rather than episodic: more than a thousand round trips a day in an actively traded instrument, each completed within a minute and often in milliseconds.

questions.stem: Low-latency traders most likely include:

options.A: News traders and certain parasitic traders.
options.B: High-frequency market-making firms exclusively.
options.C: No type of trader, since no such category exists.

rationales.A: Low-latency traders include news traders, who trade on electronic news feeds, and certain parasitic traders. Parasitic traders are speculators who base their predictions about future prices on information they obtain about orders that other traders intend, or will soon intend, to fill; they include front runners, who trade in front of traders who demand liquidity, and quote matchers, who trade in front of traders who supply liquidity. When opening or closing positions, low-latency traders often need to send or cancel orders very quickly in response to new information. In contrast to high-frequency traders, they may hold their positions for as long as a day and sometimes longer.
rationales.B: High-frequency traders are only a subset of those who compete on latency. News traders working electronic news feeds and parasitic traders such as front runners and quote matchers also depend on speed, and unlike HFTs they may hold positions for as long as a day or more.
rationales.C: The category is both defined and populated. It covers the speed-dependent strategies beyond pure high-frequency trading, including news traders and the parasitic traders who front-run liquidity demanders or match the quotes of liquidity suppliers.

questions.stem: Electronic news traders most likely:

options.A: Trade on high-speed news feeds using marketable orders.
options.B: Trade random orders unrelated to information flow.
options.C: Avoid news entirely to reduce information risk.

rationales.A: Electronic news traders subscribe to high-speed electronic news feeds that report releases made by corporations, governments, and other aggregators of information. They then quickly analyze those releases to determine whether the information will move the markets and, if so, in which direction, and they trade on it by sending marketable orders, that is, instructions to fill at the best available price, to wherever they expect to be filled. They profit when they can execute against stale orders, orders that do not yet reflect the new information.
rationales.B: Their strategy is entirely news-driven, not random: machine-readable feeds are parsed in microseconds and the direction of the trade follows from the content of the release.
rationales.C: News is the input to the strategy, not a risk to be avoided. High-speed feeds are analyzed immediately for direction and materiality, and the orders sent are marketable so as to execute against stale quotes before they are updated.

questions.stem: Electronic dealers are most likely to:

options.A: hold large inventory positions.
options.B: trade in all order sizes.
options.C: profit from round trips at favorable net spreads.

rationales.A: Electronic dealers are wary and generally will not hold large inventory positions in actively traded stocks. Those trading at the highest frequencies react to the first indication that prices may move against their inventory by immediately taking liquidity on the opposite side of the market to reduce exposure, so sizeable positions are closed out rather than carried.
rationales.B: They are market makers, but wary ones. Rather than standing ready to trade in every size, they keep inventory small in actively traded names, cut exposure as soon as prices threaten to move against them, and cancel their orders just before scheduled news releases to avoid offering liquidity to traders who can act faster than they can.
rationales.C: Electronic dealers, like all dealers, make markets by placing bids (prices at which they are willing to buy) and offers (prices at which they are willing to sell) with the expectation that they can profit from round trips at favorable net spreads. Those who trade at the highest frequencies tend to be very wary: on the first indication that prices may move against their inventory positions, they immediately take liquidity by executing on the opposite side of the market to reduce their exposure. They generally will not hold large inventory positions in actively traded stocks, and they keep track of scheduled news releases, cancelling their orders just before a release so as not to offer liquidity to traders who can act faster than they can.

questions.stem: Electronic arbitrageurs are most likely to:

options.A: find no exploitable mispricings to trade.
options.B: trade a single instrument within one market.
options.C: buy an undervalued instrument and sell a similar overvalued one.

rationales.A: Arbitrage opportunities appear continuously in electronic markets, typically at small scale and for very short periods, and a class of low-latency traders exists precisely to exploit them by buying the undervalued instrument against the sale of a similar overvalued one.
rationales.B: Comparison across markets is the essence of the strategy. The undervalued instrument and the similar overvalued one are generally found in different markets, and the two positions are combined into a single arbitrage portfolio; a strategy confined to one instrument in one market would have nothing to arbitrage.
rationales.C: Electronic arbitrageurs look across markets for arbitrage opportunities in which they can buy an undervalued instrument and sell a similar overvalued one. The combination of these two positions is called an arbitrage portfolio, and the individual positions are called legs. They try to construct their arbitrage portfolios at minimum cost and risk, which they pursue through three strategies: taking liquidity on both sides, offering liquidity on one side and taking it on the other, or offering liquidity on both sides.

questions.stem: Electronic front runners are most likely to:

options.A: be absent from modern electronic markets.
options.B: use artificial intelligence to detect same-side order flow.
options.C: trade only after other participants have filled their orders.

rationales.A: Electronic front running is a recognized low-latency strategy. Artificial intelligence methods are used to detect large orders, or many small correlated orders, on the same side of the market, and the front runner then trades ahead of that flow.
rationales.B: Electronic front runners are low-latency traders who use artificial intelligence methods to identify when large traders, or many small traders, are trying to fill orders on the same side of the market. They purchase when they believe that an imbalance of buy orders over sell orders will push the market up, and they sell when they believe the opposite. These order anticipation strategies try to identify predictable patterns in order submissions, in trades, or in the relations between trades and other events. Dealers and brokers cannot legally front run orders their own clients have submitted, but they may trade on publicly observable patterns.
rationales.C: Trading after every other participant has filled is the opposite of the strategy. The front runner's edge comes from acting ahead of the detected order flow, buying before an identified imbalance of buy orders pushes the market up and selling before the reverse.

questions.stem: Electronic quote matchers are most likely to:

options.A: follow no defined trading strategy.
options.B: trade in front of liquidity demanders.
options.C: trade in front of liquidity suppliers.

rationales.A: The strategy is well defined: quote matchers exploit the option value of standing orders, the limit orders waiting in the book to be filled, which lets them take positions with potentially limited losses.
rationales.B: Trading in front of liquidity demanders, in anticipation of their market orders, describes the electronic front runner. Quote matchers instead trade in front of the traders who supply liquidity through standing limit orders.
rationales.C: Electronic quote matchers trade in front of traders who supply liquidity, trying to exploit the option values of standing orders — limit orders waiting to be filled. Options to trade are valuable to quote matchers because they allow positions to be taken with potentially limited losses: a quote matcher buys when it believes it can rely on standing buy orders to get out of the position, and it sells when it can do the same with standing sell orders. Parasitic traders of this type divide into front runners, who trade in front of liquidity demanders, and quote matchers, who trade in front of liquidity suppliers.

questions.stem: Buy-side traders and their brokers, aware of front runners, most likely respond by:

options.A: welcoming detection of their orders.
options.B: trading at regular intervals in uniform sizes.
options.C: randomizing the timing and size of their orders.

rationales.A: Detection is the threat, not a benefit. Once a large order is identified, electronic traders trade ahead of it and the buy-side trader's fills get worse, not better.
rationales.B: Regular intervals and uniform sizes are exactly the patterns that order anticipation strategies look for, so repeating them aids the predator. The response is to randomize submissions rather than to make them predictable.
rationales.C: Buy-side traders, and the brokers who provide them with algorithms to manage large orders, are aware of the efforts that electronic traders make to detect and front run their orders. Accordingly, they randomize their strategies to make them more difficult to detect: they submit orders at random times instead of at regular intervals, and they submit various sizes instead of the same size, so that the pieces hide among other orders. These techniques make detection more difficult but not impossible, because hiding large, liquidity-demanding trades is always challenging — sophisticated traders can ultimately identify them from the inevitable relation between prices and volumes that such trades create.

drills.los_text: describe characteristics and uses of electronic trading systems

questions.stem: Algorithms used to fill orders are most likely to:

options.A: process a single simple order at a time.
options.B: submit market orders exclusively.
options.C: combine sequences of simple, advanced, and multiple orders.

rationales.A: An algorithm is a programmed strategy rather than a single order. It orchestrates combinations and sequences of orders toward an objective, and a common objective is to break one large order into many pieces submitted over time and across venues.
rationales.B: Market orders are only part of the toolkit. Algorithms draw on simple orders, limit orders, advanced order types and routing across multiple venues, choosing among them as the objective and the state of the market require.
rationales.C: Algorithms (algos for short) are programmed strategies for filling orders, and they may use combinations or sequences of simple orders, advanced orders, or multiple orders to achieve their objectives. Buy-side traders use algorithms, often provided by brokers, extensively both to trade small orders and to reduce the price impacts of large trades. Many algorithms break up a large order and submit the pieces to various markets over time, which makes it difficult for other traders to infer that a trader is trying to fill a large order. The pieces are typically submitted at random times, in random sizes, and sometimes to randomly selected exchanges, to hide their common origin.

questions.stem: VWAP algorithms are most likely to:

options.A: trade only at the market close.
options.B: match the volume-weighted average price over a set interval.
options.C: trade only at the market open.

rationales.A: Concentrating all execution at the close ignores the volume distribution the algorithm is built to track. The algorithm spreads execution across the whole interval in proportion to expected volume, targeting the interval's volume-weighted average price or better.
rationales.B: VWAP algorithms attempt to obtain a volume-weighted average fill price that is close to, or better than, the volume-weighted average price (VWAP) of all trades arranged within a prespecified time interval. To minimize the variation between the actual average fill price and the VWAP over the interval, these algorithms try to participate in an equal fraction of all trading volume throughout the interval, forecasting volumes from the historical volume profile and from current volumes. The algorithm therefore trades more during periods of historically high volume, such as around the market open and close, and when the market has been more active than normal, and it trades less during periods of relatively low volume.
rationales.C: Open-only execution ignores the remainder of the day's volume. The algorithm participates throughout the interval, trading more when volume is historically high — including the open and the close — and less when volume is low, so that its fill price tracks the interval VWAP.

questions.stem: An immediate or cancel (IOC) limit order is most likely to:

options.A: cancel if it finds no liquidity.
options.B: rest hidden in the book until filled.
options.C: convert to a market order if unfilled.

rationales.A: The immediate or cancel (IOC) limit order is by far the most common order type in electronic markets. Traders use these orders to discover hidden orders that may stand in the spread between a market's quoted bid and ask prices. Because an IOC order cancels immediately if it does not find liquidity, it never rests in the book; it is therefore itself hidden and does not reveal the submitting trader's intentions.
rationales.B: Resting in the book until fully filled describes a standing hidden limit order. An IOC order never rests: it cancels immediately if it does not find liquidity, which is precisely why it too is hidden and does not reveal trade intentions.
rationales.C: An unfilled IOC order is cancelled, not converted into a market order; converting it would force execution at whatever price was available and would expose the trader's intentions. Traders use IOC orders to probe for hidden orders standing in the spread while revealing nothing about their own trading plans.

questions.stem: Pinging the market is best described as:

options.A: a small IOC limit order probing for hidden orders.
options.B: a large order worked for immediate execution.
options.C: a practice not found in electronic markets.

rationales.A: Some electronic traders try to discover hidden orders by pinging the market: they submit a small immediate or cancel limit order for only a few shares at the price at which they are looking for hidden orders. If the pinging order trades, they know that a hidden order is present at that price; they do not, however, learn its full size, which can be discovered only by trading with it. Traders then may use this information to adjust their trading strategies.
rationales.B: The pinging order is deliberately small — only a few shares — because its purpose is to probe for liquidity, not to execute size. A large order would move the price and reveal the trader's intentions, which is the opposite of what the probe is for.
rationales.C: Pinging is a common practice in electronic markets, and it is the standard way of testing whether a hidden order stands at a given price.

questions.stem: Flickering quotes are best described as:

options.A: permanent standing limit orders.
options.B: exposed limit orders cancelled within a second.
options.C: orders not seen in electronic markets.

rationales.A: Flickering quotes are very short-lived, often cancelled within a second of submission, which is the opposite of a permanent standing order. The whole point is that the order is seen but does not stand in the market.
rationales.B: Electronic markets often have flickering quotes, which are exposed limit orders that electronic traders submit and then cancel shortly thereafter, often within a second. Electronic dealers and algorithmic buy-side traders submit and repeatedly cancel and resubmit these orders when they do not want their orders to stand in the market but do want other traders to see that they are willing to trade at the displayed price. A trader who wishes to trade with a flickering quote can place a hidden limit order at the price where the quote is flickering; if the flickering order returns, it will hit that hidden limit order.
rationales.C: Flickering quotes are common in electronic markets, a routine consequence of electronic dealers and algorithmic buy-side traders repeatedly submitting and cancelling exposed limit orders rather than letting them stand.

questions.stem: Leapfrog behavior most likely occurs when:

options.A: Spreads are narrow.
options.B: Bid-ask spreads are wide.
options.C: The spread is exactly zero.

rationales.A: Leapfrog requires room between the bid and the offer. When spreads are narrow, there is no scope for a dealer to improve repeatedly on another trader's quote and still trade at a favorable price, so the jumping-ahead sequence never gets started. Leapfrog is a wide-spread phenomenon.
rationales.B: When bid-ask spreads are wide, dealers often are willing to trade at better prices than they quote. They quote wide spreads because they hope to trade at more favorable prices. When another trader quotes a better price, dealers often immediately quote an even better price. For example, if the market is 20 bid, offered at 28, and a buy-side trader bids at 21, a dealer might instantly bid at 22. This behavior frustrates buy-side traders, who then must quote a better price to maintain order precedence. If the spread is sufficiently wide, a game of leapfrog may ensue as the dealer jumps ahead again.
rationales.C: A spread of exactly zero leaves nothing to improve on: the bid already equals the offer, so no dealer can quote a better price and no one can jump ahead. Leapfrog arises at the opposite extreme, where the spread is wide enough that a dealer can keep stepping in front of an improving quote and still trade profitably.

questions.stem: Machine learning in electronic trading is most likely effective when:

options.A: Problems repeat regularly and often.
options.B: Problems are entirely novel.
options.C: Volatility is extreme.

rationales.A: Machine learning, also known as data mining, uses advanced statistical methods to characterize data structures, producing models based on observed empirical regularities rather than on theoretical principles identified by analysts. These methods can be powerful when stable processes generate vast amounts of data, such as occurs in active financial markets. Many trading problems are ideally suited to machine-learning analyses because the problems repeat regularly and often, and for such problems machine-based learning systems can be extraordinarily powerful. The same systems are often useless, or worse, when trading becomes extraordinary and volatilities shoot up, because those episodes have few precedents from which the machines can learn.
rationales.B: Because these methods learn from observed empirical regularities rather than from theory, they need many precedents to generalize from. A genuinely novel problem supplies none. Machine learning is effective over stable processes that generate vast amounts of data on repeating problems, not over one-off situations.
rationales.C: Machine-learning systems are often useless, or worse, when trading becomes extraordinary, for example when volatilities shoot up, because these episodes have few precedents from which the machines can learn. Many traders shut their systems down when volatility spikes. Extreme volatility is therefore the condition under which the approach performs poorly, not the condition under which it is effective.

drills.los_text: describe comparative advantages of low-latency traders

questions.stem: In electronic trading, the three major steps in reacting to an event are most likely to:

options.A: learn of the event, respond with a new order instruction, then send it to the exchange.
options.B: receive the exchange's data feed, confirm the event, then await a request for instructions.
options.C: send a new order instruction, learn whether the event took place, then compute a response.

rationales.A: Reacting to an event consists of three major steps: the trader must learn that the event took place; the trader must respond to the new information with a new order instruction; and the trader must send, and the exchange must receive, the new instruction. Traders use very fast communication systems to minimize the latencies associated with steps 1 and 3, communicating in and out, and very fast computer systems to minimize the latency associated with step 2, responding.
rationales.B: Traders respond unilaterally with new order instructions; they do not confirm events with the exchange or wait for it to request instructions. The three steps are learning that the event took place, responding with a new order instruction, and sending it for the exchange to receive.
rationales.C: The sequence is scrambled: the trader must first learn that the event occurred (step 1), then respond with a new order instruction (step 2), and only then send it for the exchange to receive (step 3). Fast communications minimize the latency of steps 1 and 3; fast computers minimize the latency of step 2.

questions.stem: Collocation is most likely:

options.A: The placing of traders' servers in the exchange's server room.
options.B: A practice that does not exist in electronic markets.
options.C: A practice banned by securities regulators in major markets.

rationales.A: Many exchanges allow electronic traders to place their servers in the rooms where the exchange servers operate, a practice called collocation. Exchanges charge substantial fees for collocation space and related services, such as air conditioning and power. Even within collocation centers, concerns about fairness dictate that the communication lines connecting proprietary servers to exchange servers all be of the same length for all customers buying the same class of collocation service.
rationales.B: Collocation is standard practice: traders' servers are placed in the exchange's own data center to minimize transmission latency, and exchanges charge substantial fees for the space, power and cooling involved.
rationales.C: Collocation is legal and is commercially offered by exchanges, which sell the space and related services openly. Regulatory attention goes to fairness within the facility, so the communication lines from proprietary servers to exchange servers must be of equal length for every customer buying the same class of service, rather than to prohibiting the practice.

questions.stem: Communication distances matter most likely because:

options.A: Router and switch latencies dominate transmission distance.
options.B: Signals travel faster through optical fiber than through air.
options.C: No message can travel faster than the speed of light.

rationales.A: Equipment latencies add to, but do not eliminate, the physical limit. Each router and switch a message passes through adds its own latency, which is why traders minimize the number of such devices in the line, but round-trip transmission between Chicago and New York still takes about 8 ms and between New York and London about 37 ms simply because of the speed of light over those distances.
rationales.B: This reverses the fact: the speed of light in standard optical fiber is about 31% slower than in a vacuum, which is why traders prefer line-of-sight microwave channels through air. The fundamental constraint is not the medium's advantage but that no message can travel faster than the speed of light over the distance involved.
rationales.C: Electronic traders and brokers locate their computers as close as possible to the exchanges at which they trade to minimize latencies resulting from physics: no message can travel faster than the speed of light. At 300,000 kilometers (186,000 miles) per second in a vacuum, light travels 300 kilometers in a millisecond. The great circle, or shortest, distances between Chicago and New York and between New York and London are 1,146 kilometers and 5,576 kilometers, so round-trip communications between these pairs of cities have minimum latencies of approximately 8 and 37 milliseconds simply because of the speed of light. The actual minimum latencies are longer because the speed of light in standard optical fiber is 31% slower than in a vacuum. No trader at any significant distance from the information source or the trading venue can effectively compete with traders who have minimized their combined distances.

questions.stem: Line-of-sight microwave channels most likely are preferred to fiber-optic and copper because:

options.A: Microwaves travel through air at nearly the speed of light.
options.B: Microwave transmission is slower but cheaper to operate.
options.C: Microwaves offer no speed advantage over fiber-optic cable.

rationales.A: Electronic traders and brokers use the fastest and most direct communication lines available to collect and transmit information when distance separates the places where information events occur from the places where they act on them. They prefer line-of-sight microwave channels to fiber-optic and copper channels because of the difference in the speed of electromagnetic wave propagation through these materials: microwaves travel through air at just slightly below the speed of light, whereas signals travel through fiber-optic channels and copper wires only two-thirds as quickly. They also ensure that their communications pass through the fewest electronic routers and switches possible, because passage through each of these devices adds its latency to the total latency of the line.
rationales.B: The direction is wrong. Microwaves through air travel at just under the speed of light, while signals in fiber-optic channels and copper wires propagate only about two-thirds as quickly, so microwave channels are the faster medium. Speed, not operating cost, is why latency-sensitive traders buy them.
rationales.C: The speed difference is the entire rationale for the preference: microwaves through air propagate at just below the speed of light against roughly two-thirds of that in fiber-optic and copper channels. If there were no speed advantage, traders would have no reason to pay for line-of-sight microwave links.

questions.stem: The techniques electronic traders use to achieve fast computation most likely include:

options.A: Neither hardware nor software optimization.
options.B: Deliberately underclocked processors.
options.C: Overclocked processors and assembler code for repeated functions.

rationales.A: Optimization is comprehensive rather than absent. Traders store all information in fast memory to avoid the latencies of physical disk drives, use specialized processors designed for their specific trading problems, run simple specialized operating systems to avoid unused operating system overhead, and optimize their code for speed. Exchange matching engines do not equalize participants, which is precisely why this effort pays.
rationales.B: The direction is the opposite: traders overclock their processors, running them faster than the designers intended, and use liquid cooling systems to keep them from melting. Thermal stability is bought with cooling, not with lower clock speeds.
rationales.C: Electronic traders use very fast computers. They overclock their processors, running them faster than the processor designers intended, and use liquid cooling systems to keep them from melting. They store all information in fast memory to avoid the latencies associated with physical disk drives.
