They sometimes use specialized processors designed to solve their specific trading problems quickly, and may even use processors etched on gallium arsenide rather than silicon. They also must run very efficient software, often using simple and specialized operating systems to avoid the overhead of operating system functions they do not use; many electronic trading systems run under variants of the original MS-DOS operating system because of its simplicity. They optimize their code for speed, often writing important functions that they use repeatedly in assembler language to ensure that those functions run quickly, and they avoid interpreter languages such as Python for time-critical code.

questions.stem: Contingency tables in electronic trading most likely:

options.A: Contain prearranged action plans.
options.B: Serve no purpose in latency-sensitive trading.
options.C: Waste time on events that may never occur.

rationales.A: Some electronic traders reduce latency by creating contingency tables that contain prearranged action plans. Suppose a bid rises in a market in which electronic traders are active. In response to the increased bid, traders may want to raise their own bids or offers, and that decision may depend on their inventory positions and on many other factors. Deciding what to do following an increased bid may require substantial analyses, which take time. Traders can reduce their decision latencies by doing these analyses before the bid increases instead of afterward: seeing the increased bid, they simply look up the optimal response in a contingency table stored in memory. To be most useful, the tables must be kept up to date and must include responses for the most likely events.
rationales.B: The purpose of a contingency table is exactly decision-latency reduction: the analysis is done in advance, so the response to an observed event is a table lookup in memory rather than a fresh calculation.
rationales.C: Pre-computation is where the saving comes from, not where time is lost. The analysis is performed before the event rather than after it, and the tables are limited to responses for the most likely events and kept up to date, so the work done ahead of time is the work that would otherwise sit on the critical path.

questions.stem: The ideal use of Python by electronic traders most likely is:

options.A: Never, in any trading code.
options.B: Always, for maximum execution speed.
options.C: When speed of coding matters more than speed of execution.

rationales.A: Python does have a role. Some electronic trading problems change so frequently that speed of coding is more important than speed of execution, and for those problems traders use high-level languages such as Python because they can code faster and more accurately in them than in lower-level languages such as C++.
rationales.B: Python is not the choice for pure execution speed. Traders avoid such languages for time-critical code because they are interpreter languages that compile, that is, create executable machine code, as they run, rather than compiling only once when first written. Repeatedly used time-critical functions are written in assembler or other low-level languages instead.
rationales.C: Traders avoid languages such as Python for time-critical work because they are interpreter languages that compile as they run rather than compiling only once when first written. However, some electronic trading problems change so frequently that speed of coding is more important than speed of execution; for example, some problems depend on ever-changing sets of conditions or exceptions that present or constrain profit opportunities. For such problems, traders use high-level languages such as Python, because they can code faster and more accurately in these languages than in lower-level languages such as C++. If they expect that the software will remain useful, they may later recode those routines in other languages to make them run faster.

drills.los_text: describe the risks associated with electronic trading and how regulators mitigate them

questions.stem: The HFT arms race most likely creates:

options.A: Barriers to entry that can create natural monopolies.
options.B: No barriers to entry.
options.C: Unlimited competition among traders.

rationales.A: Competition among high-frequency traders has created an arms race in which each trader tries to be faster than the next. Consequently, the state-of-the-art high-frequency trading technologies necessary to compete successfully are now very expensive, making entry quite costly. These costs form barriers to entry that can create natural monopolies. Although substantial evidence suggests that electronic trading benefits the markets, these benefits may erode if only a few high-frequency traders survive and can exploit their unique positions. Many high-frequency traders are already quitting the markets because they cannot compete effectively.
rationales.B: The barriers are real and economic. The state-of-the-art technologies needed to compete on speed are now very expensive, which makes entry costly and keeps new competitors out.
rationales.C: The arms race concentrates the field rather than opening it. Many high-frequency traders are already quitting because they cannot compete effectively, and the benefits of electronic trading may erode if only a few survive and can exploit their unique positions.

questions.stem: Systemic risks of electronic trading are most likely:

options.A: fully compensated by the entity responsible.
options.B: harmful beyond the entity responsible for the failure.
options.C: absent from electronic markets.

rationales.A: Systemic risks are uncompensated. They are particularly problematic precisely because the entity responsible for a failure is often not required, or is unable, to compensate the others on whom its failure imposes costs. When people do not bear the full costs of their behaviors, they tend not to be as careful in avoiding damaging behaviors as they otherwise would be, so treating these risks as fully compensated misses the core of the problem.
rationales.B: A systemic risk is a risk that some failure will hurt more than just the entity responsible for the failure. Electronic trading created new systemic risks of this kind, and they concern regulators and practitioners. Such risks are particularly problematic when the responsible entity is not required or is unable to compensate others for the costs its failure imposes on them, because people who do not bear the full costs of their behaviors tend not to be as careful in avoiding damaging behaviors as they otherwise would be. The systemic risks associated with fast trading may be caused by electronic exchange trading system failures or by excessive orders submitted by electronic traders.
rationales.C: These are real risks, not hypothetical ones. Electronic exchange trading system failures and excessive order submission by electronic traders have both imposed costs on parties other than the firm at fault, which is why regulators and practitioners treat systemic risk as a distinct category of concern in electronic markets.

questions.stem: The Knight Capital trading failure of 1 August 2012 is best described as:

options.A: a runaway algorithm sending unintended orders.
options.B: a minor incident of limited financial consequence.
options.C: a manual order entry error by a human trader.

rationales.A: Runaway algorithms produce streams of unintended orders that result from programming mistakes, and the problems sometimes occur when programmers do not anticipate some contingency. The Knight Capital trading failure on 1 August 2012 may be the most extreme example of a runaway algorithm incident. Owing to a software programming mistake, Knight sent millions of orders to the markets over a 45-minute period when it intended only to fill 212 orders, some of which normally might have been broken up but none of which would have generated so many orders. Those orders produced 4 million executions involving 397 stocks, and Knight lost $400 million in the incident.
rationales.B: The event was near-fatal to the firm rather than minor. Knight lost $400 million in well under an hour, from 4 million executions involving 397 stocks, which is among the largest losses ever produced by a single trading technology failure.
rationales.C: The cause was software rather than a mis-keyed manual order. A software programming mistake sent millions of orders to the markets over a 45-minute period when Knight intended only to fill 212 orders. An order larger than intended, entered by hand because a trader hits the wrong key or hits a key more often than intended, is a fat finger error, which is a separate failure mode.

questions.stem: The 6 May 2010 Flash Crash is best described as:

options.A: an overlarge algorithmic order in index futures.
options.B: a slow, orderly decline spread evenly across the session.
options.C: a disruption with no single identifiable trigger.

rationales.A: Overlarge orders demand more liquidity than the market can provide. In these events a trader, often inexperienced, tries to execute a marketable order that is too large for the market to handle without severely disrupting prices in the time given to fill the order. The 6 May 2010 Flash Crash occurred as a result of such an order. It was triggered when a large institutional trader tried to sell $4.1 billion in E-mini S&P 500 futures contracts using an algorithm over a short period, where the algorithm was designed to participate in a fixed fraction of market volume. When the initial trades depressed S&P 500 futures prices, trading volumes increased substantially as arbitrageurs and others started to trade. The increase in trading volumes caused the algorithm to increase the rate of its order submissions, which exacerbated the problem. The market reverted to its former levels after the Chicago Mercantile Exchange briefly halted trading in the E-mini S&P 500 futures contract, and the large order eventually was filled. The E-mini fell roughly 5% in about five minutes and then recovered nearly fully.
rationales.B: The crash was fast rather than gradual. The E-mini S&P 500 contract fell roughly 5% in about five minutes and then recovered nearly fully once the Chicago Mercantile Exchange briefly halted trading in it, which is the opposite of a slow decline spread evenly across the session.
rationales.C: The event was traced to a specific trigger: one institutional trader's attempt to sell $4.1 billion of E-mini S&P 500 futures through an algorithm designed to participate in a fixed fraction of market volume, whose order submissions accelerated as the volume it caused increased.

questions.stem: Fat finger errors are best described as:

options.A: errors whose consequences are smaller in electronic markets.
options.B: errors unique to electronic trading systems.
options.C: orders larger than the trader intended.

rationales.A: The consequences are often greater in electronic systems, not smaller, because of the speed at which those systems operate and because the clerks who often catch such errors in manual trading systems, before they cause problems, are not present in an electronic workflow.
rationales.B: These errors are not unique to electronic trading systems. A manual trader can submit an order larger than intended in any market, by hitting the wrong key or hitting a key more often than intended. What electronic trading changes is the size of the consequence, not whether the error is possible.
rationales.C: Fat finger errors occur when a manual trader submits a larger order than intended. They are called fat finger errors because they sometimes occur when a trader hits the wrong key or hits a key more often than intended. These types of errors are not unique to electronic trading systems, but their consequences are often greater in electronic systems because of the speed at which they operate and because clerks often catch these errors in manual trading systems before they cause problems.

questions.stem: Malevolent order streams are most likely:

options.A: accidental in every case.
options.B: nonexistent in practice.
options.C: deliberately created to disrupt markets.

rationales.A: They are deliberate rather than accidental. The perpetrators may be market manipulators; aggrieved employees, such as traders or software engineers; or terrorists. An unintended stream of orders produced by a programming mistake is a runaway algorithm, which is a different failure from a malevolent order stream.
rationales.B: The threat is a real one. Traders conducting denial-of-service attacks designed to overwhelm their competitors' electronic trading systems with excessive quotes also may create malevolent order streams, alongside manipulators, aggrieved employees and terrorists.
rationales.C: Malevolent order streams are created deliberately to disrupt the markets. The perpetrators may be market manipulators; aggrieved employees, such as traders or software engineers; or terrorists. Traders conducting denial-of-service attacks designed to overwhelm their competitors' electronic trading systems with excessive quotes also may create malevolent order streams.

questions.stem: A solution to the systemic risks of electronic trading is most likely to:

options.A: permit sponsored naked access for client orders.
options.B: test trading software thoroughly before live use.
options.C: rely on post-trade audits instead of real-time surveillance.

rationales.A: This is the opposite of the guidance. Brokers must surveil all client orders, and they must not allow their clients to enter orders directly into exchange trading systems, a process called sponsored naked access.
rationales.B: The solutions to the systemic risk problems associated with electronic trading systems are multifold. Most obviously, traders must test software thoroughly before using it in live trading, and exchanges often conduct mock trading sessions to allow developers to test their software. Rigorous market access controls must ensure that only orders coming from approved sources enter electronic order-matching systems. Rigorous access controls on software developers must ensure that only authorized developers can change software, and best practice mandates that all software be read, understood and vouched for by at least one developer besides its author. The electronic traders who generate orders and the electronic exchanges that receive them must surveil their order flow in real time to ensure it conforms to preset parameters. Brokers must surveil all client orders and must not allow sponsored naked access. Some exchanges have also adopted price limits and trade halts to stop trading when prices move too quickly.
rationales.C: Electronic traders who generate orders, and the electronic exchanges that receive them, must surveil their order flow in real time to ensure it conforms to preset parameters. Real-time surveillance is both feasible and expected practice, and an after-the-fact audit on its own cannot stop a malfunctioning system quickly enough to prevent the damage.

questions.stem: Trade halts are most likely:

options.A: absent from exchange rules.
options.B: harmful to market quality.
options.C: triggered when prices move too quickly.

rationales.A: Price limits and trade halts are common practice. Some exchanges have adopted them precisely to stop trading when prices move too quickly, so they are a feature of exchange rules rather than something unavailable.
rationales.B: They have a protective role rather than a harmful one. They stop trading when excess demands for liquidity occur, and they prevent the extreme price changes that can occur in electronic markets when market orders arrive and no liquidity is present.
rationales.C: Some exchanges have adopted price limits and trade halts to stop trading when prices move too quickly. These rules stop trading when excess demands for liquidity occur, and they also prevent the extreme price changes that can occur in electronic markets when market orders arrive and no liquidity is present. For the same reason, most brokers now automatically convert market orders into marketable limit orders to ensure that they do not trade at unreasonable prices.

drills.los_text: describe abusive trading practices that real-time surveillance of markets may detect

questions.stem: The goal of real-time market surveillance is most likely to:

options.A: replace brokers' surveillance of their clients' orders.
options.B: review order flow in overnight batches after the close.
options.C: detect potential market abuse while it is happening.

rationales.A: Real-time market surveillance complements broker-level monitoring rather than replacing it. Brokers must still surveil all of their clients' orders, while exchanges and regulators monitor the aggregate order flow. The aim of the surveillance itself is to detect potential market abuse as it occurs.
rationales.B: A review run in overnight batches after the close is not real-time surveillance. The goal is to detect potential abuse while it is happening, because real-time monitoring allows faster responses to potential crises and market abuses, with the potential for rapid intervention to prevent or minimize damages.
rationales.C: Regulators around the world recognize that real-time market monitoring and surveillance systems allow faster responses to potential crises and market abuses, with the potential for rapid intervention to prevent or minimize damages. The goal of real-time market surveillance is to detect potential market abuse while it is happening. Real-time surveillance often can detect front running; market manipulation, whose strategies include bluffing, gunning, squeezing and cornering; trading for market impact; rumormongering; wash trading; and spoofing.

questions.stem: Front running is best described as:

options.A: a practice that is legal in every jurisdiction.
options.B: a practice that does not occur in real markets.
options.C: buying ahead of anticipated purchases and selling ahead of anticipated sales.

rationales.A: Legality depends on how the information was obtained. In most jurisdictions, front running is illegal if the front runners acquire their information about orders improperly, for example by a tip from a broker handling a large order. The same strategy is legal if the information on which it is based is properly obtained, for example by watching a market data feed.
rationales.B: Front running is a real and recognized practice, legal or illegal depending on the source of the information behind it. Some traders use electronic artificial intelligence systems to identify when traders are filling large orders over time by breaking them up into small pieces, and then trade ahead on the same side.
rationales.C: Front running involves buying in front of anticipated purchases and selling in front of anticipated sales. In most jurisdictions, front running is illegal if the front runners acquire their information about orders improperly, for example by a tip from a broker handling a large order. Some traders use electronic artificial intelligence systems to identify when traders are filling large orders over time by breaking them up into small pieces; when these traders suspect that buyers or sellers are working large orders, they will trade ahead on the same side with the hope of benefiting when the large traders move prices as they fill their orders. This front-running strategy is legal if the information on which it is based is properly obtained, for example by watching a market data feed. Front running increases transaction costs for the traders whose orders are front run.

questions.stem: Rumormongering is best described as:

options.A: an unrecognized category of market abuse.
options.B: the spread of false information to alter value assessments.
options.C: legally protected expression of opinion.

rationales.A: Rumormongering is a recognized form of market abuse, namely the dissemination of false information about fundamental values or about other traders' trading intentions, and it is one of the behaviors real-time market surveillance is meant to detect.
rationales.B: Rumormongering is the dissemination of false information about fundamental values or about other traders' trading intentions to alter investors' value assessments. It is illegal in most jurisdictions. Financial analysts must be careful to ensure that they base their analyses on valid information and not on false information designed to fool them into making poor decisions. Note that although rumormongering is illegal in most jurisdictions, simply reporting one side of an issue is not illegal; analysts must therefore also ensure that they base their analyses on balanced information and not on information that is true but selectively presented to them with the purpose of distorting their analyses.
rationales.C: Disseminating false information in order to move valuations is market manipulation, illegal in most jurisdictions, rather than protected opinion. The narrower point is that reporting only one side of an issue is not illegal, which is why analysts must insist on balanced as well as valid information.

questions.stem: Wash trading in a security is most likely described as:

options.A: Misreported prices on trades that did occur.
options.B: Arranged trades among commonly controlled accounts.
options.C: Repeated trades at one price between unrelated parties.

rationales.A: Wash trades are real trades, arranged among commonly controlled accounts so that no economic ownership actually changes hands. The related abuse of false reporting involves reporting trades that never occurred at all, not merely misstating the prices of trades that did occur, and it is not confined to prices while leaving volumes accurate. Misreporting the price of a genuine trade between unrelated parties is a reporting violation, but it is not what makes a trade a wash trade: common control of both sides is.
rationales.B: Wash trading consists of trades arranged among commonly controlled accounts to create the impression of market activity at a particular price. The purpose is to fool investors into believing that a market is more liquid than it truly is and thereby to increase investors' confidence both in their ability to exit positions without substantial cost and in their assessments of security values. Manipulators can achieve the same purposes by falsely reporting trades that never occurred, which is essentially what happens when they arrange trades among accounts they control on both sides.
rationales.C: Trades between genuinely unrelated parties that happen to execute repeatedly at the same price are ordinary market activity; a stable execution price simply reflects agreement about value. Wash trading requires that the accounts on both sides be commonly controlled, which is what makes the apparent activity fictitious and the displayed liquidity illusory.

questions.stem: Spoofing (also called layering) is most likely:

options.A: A hidden-order strategy for concealing trading intentions.
options.B: Not a recognized practice in electronic markets.
options.C: An exposed-order strategy for misstating liquidity or value.

rationales.A: Spoofing works through exposed standing limit orders: visibility is the mechanism of the deception, because other traders must see the orders in order to be misled by them. Hidden orders do the opposite and conceal intentions. A spoofer typically combines the two, placing a hidden order on the side he genuinely wants to trade and displaying the deceptive orders on the opposite side.
rationales.B: Spoofing, also called layering, is a recognized and prosecuted abuse in electronic markets. Displayed liquidity that the trader never intends to execute, and cancels once it has moved others, is the core of the practice.
rationales.C: Spoofing, also known as layering, is a trading practice in which traders place exposed standing limit orders to convey an impression to other traders that the market is more liquid than it is, or to suggest to other traders that the security is under- or overvalued. For example, suppose a spoofer wants to buy stock cheaply or quickly. The spoofer might place a hidden buy order in the market, then place one or more exposed sell limit orders to convey the impression that prices may soon fall. Seeing the spoofing sell orders, one or more traders may conclude that values are lower than market prices suggest and sell into the spoofer's buy order, enabling the spoofer to obtain a quick and possibly cheaper purchase; the spoofer then cancels the exposed sell orders.

questions.stem: Bluffing in a pump-and-dump scheme is most likely described as:

options.A: Placing hidden orders to conceal trading intentions.
options.B: Submitting orders to influence other traders' perceptions of value.
options.C: Buying after valid positive news to correct an undervaluation.

rationales.A: Hiding orders to avoid revealing trading intentions is a legitimate defensive tactic, used by large traders to limit the price impact of an order they intend to execute. Bluffing works in the open: the bluffer must submit visible orders and arrange trades precisely so that other traders see them and revise their perceptions of value.
rationales.B: Bluffing involves submitting orders and arranging trades to influence other traders' perceptions of value. Bluffers often prey on momentum traders, who buy when prices are rising and sell when prices are falling. In a typical pump-and-dump scheme, bluffers buy stock to raise its price and thereby encourage momentum traders to buy, then sell the stock to those momentum traders at higher prices. To further the scheme, bluffers may engage in such activities as rumormongering or wash trading. Similar manipulations run from the short side are called short and distorts.
rationales.C: Buying because valid positive news has left a security undervalued is legitimate informed trading, and it pushes price toward value rather than away from it. Bluffers may time their purchases to immediately follow the release of valid positive information, but the purpose is to fool other traders into overvaluing the material significance of that information so the bluffer can sell into their buying at inflated prices.

questions.stem: Gunning the market most likely is:

options.A: Not a recognized manipulation strategy.
options.B: Manipulative selling to trigger clustered stop-loss orders.
options.C: Legitimate liquidity provision in stressed conditions.

rationales.A: Gunning the market is a recognized manipulation, grouped with squeezing and cornering as schemes manipulators use to force other traders into disadvantageous trades.
rationales.B: Gunning the market is a strategy used by market manipulators to force traders to do disadvantageous trades. A manipulator generally guns the market by selling quickly to push prices down with the hope of triggering stop-loss sell orders. A stop-loss (or stop) sell order becomes valid for execution once the specified stop price condition is met by a trade occurring at or below the stop price. For example, suppose a manipulator believes that traders have placed many stop-loss sell orders at 50; those orders would become valid upon a trade occurring at 50 or below. The manipulator may sell aggressively to push prices down from 51 to 50 and thereby trigger the stop-loss sell orders, then profit by repurchasing at the lower prices that the forced selling produces.
rationales.C: Selling fast in order to drive the price through a cluster of stop levels and force other traders to sell is abuse, not liquidity provision. A liquidity provider posts orders on the side the market needs and earns the spread; the manipulator's trades are placed to move the price against other traders and are then reversed at their expense.

questions.stem: Squeezing and cornering are most likely:

options.A: Legal exercises of market power by far-sighted traders.
options.B: Obsolete practices eliminated by position limits and surveillance.
options.C: Schemes that withhold the resources needed to settle contracts.

rationales.A: Obtaining control of the resources necessary to settle trading contracts and then withdrawing them in order to force counterparties into disadvantageous trades is illegal manipulation in most jurisdictions. It is not a protected exercise of market power, and it is not accumulation on superior foresight: the profit comes from the counterparties' inability to perform, not from a view on value.
rationales.B: Both schemes persist, particularly around deliverable contracts. Position limits and electronic surveillance constrain them but have not eliminated them; short squeezes and commodity corners continue to be attempted and prosecuted.
rationales.C: Squeezing, cornering, and gunning the market are all schemes that market manipulators use to force traders to do disadvantageous trades. In a squeeze or corner, the manipulator obtains control over resources necessary to settle trading contracts, then unexpectedly withdraws those resources from the market, which causes traders to default on their contracts, some of which the manipulator may hold. In short squeezes, manipulators obtain control of a substantial fraction of all available lendable shares or bonds; if the securities are overvalued, many speculators may be short selling them by unknowingly borrowing from the manipulators. The manipulators then recall the security loans, and short sellers who cannot borrow elsewhere are forced to buy in the market to cover. In commodity market corners, manipulators buy many futures contracts while simultaneously buying much of the deliverable supply in the spot market. Corners are illegal in most jurisdictions.
